en: The Sūtra on the Appearance of the Four Kinds of Persons in the World, translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit, mounted on a feather-adorned chariot and surrounded by his ministers, departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the park where the World-Honored One was staying. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and desired to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:
"There are four types of persons who appear in the world. What are these four?"

Furthermore, there are some who are first ugly and later beautiful; some who are first beautiful and later ugly; some who are first ugly and later ugly; and some who are first beautiful and later beautiful.
"What is it for a person to be ugly at first and beautiful later?

Or again, there is a person born into a low and base family—whether a family of *caṇḍālas*, or executioners, or artisans, or barbers, or a poor household—in a place where there is no grain or rice and food does not suffice for the mouth; though they obtain food, it is foul, putrid, and wretched."
Born into such a family, with an appearance that is ugly and wretched, one is unpleasant for others to behold and is held in contempt; yet, one acts virtuously in body, speech, and mind.

Having cultivated wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, when he sees a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, he immediately gives rise to a humble mind, serving and honoring them without failing to observe the proper timing.
If one sees someone making offerings, upon seeing them, they feel joy and exultation; at the end of life, they will be reborn in a good place, in the heavens.

It is like a person who goes from the ground to a small bed, from a small bed to a large bed, from a large bed to a horse, from a horse to an elephant, and from an elephant to a great lecture hall. For this reason, I say that such a person was formerly ugly but later becomes sublime.
In this way, that person was first ugly and later beautiful.
"What is the person who is first beautiful and later ugly?

Suppose there is a person born into a noble and honored family, or a great clan of Kṣatriyas, a great clan of Brāhmaṇas, or a great clan of householders; or into a royal family, a family of crown princes, or a family of high ministers and other great houses—possessing a countenance so upright and peerless that its complexion is like the peach blossom."

That person then engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; when he sees śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or elders, having seen them, he has no heart of reverence, nor does he pay them homage or serve them, nor does he engage in conversation with them.

If he sees someone making an offering, upon seeing it, he immediately gives rise to a mind of jealousy. This is comprised of wrong view and doubt; thus he possesses wrong view, thinking: "There is no giving, nor is there merit, nor is there one who receives; there are no wholesome or unwholesome deeds, nor is there this world or a future world; there is no father and no mother; and in this world there are no Arhats or others who practice sublime conduct, swiftly attaining realization and dwelling in bliss."

Because he possesses this accomplishment of evil and false views, at the time of his death he will be reborn in the three evil realms within the hells—just as that man descended from the lecture hall down to the neck of an elephant, from the elephant to a horse, from the horse to a large couch, from the large couch to a small couch, and finally fell headlong from the small couch to the ground. For this reason, I say that such a person is "excellent first and ugly later."
In this way, that person is beautiful at first and ugly later.
What kind of person is ugly both at first and later?

There may be someone born into a lowly family, such as a family of *caṇḍālas*, or executioners, or artisans, or those who shave hair and beards, or others who are poor and destitute, lacking food and drink; and even when they do obtain food, it is foul-smelling, filthy, and difficult to taste.
Born into such a family, he commits evil deeds with his body, evil deeds with his speech, and evil deeds with his mind.

Having committed evil deeds with his body, speech, and mind, when he encounters śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or venerable elders, he neither shows them respect nor serves them, nor does he engage in conversation with them. He holds wrong views and is possessed by doubt, maintaining this perspective: "There is no giving, no merit, and no recipient; there is no fruit or retribution for good or evil deeds; there is no present world nor a future world; there is no father and no mother; and in this world there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have attained perfection through their practice, nor are there any arhats who, in this life or the next, have swiftly realized the superknowledges and dwell in bliss therein."
Being possessed of evil views, at the time of death he is reborn in the three miserable destinies and enters hell.
It is as if a person goes from darkness to darkness, from obscurity to obscurity; for this reason, it is said that this person is ugly first and ugly later.
In this way, that person is ugly at first and ugly later.
What kind of person is beautiful at first and beautiful later?

Suppose there is a person born into a noble and honored family, a great kṣatriya clan, a great brāhmaṇa clan, a great householder clan, a royal family, a family of a crown prince, or a family of a high minister; one who is extremely wealthy, possessing abundant riches and many treasures, and who is exceedingly handsome beyond compare, with a complexion like the peach blossom.
He cultivates wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind.

Having cultivated wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind, when he sees śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or various elders and dignitaries, he pays them respect, honors them, serves them, and provides for them; and when he sees someone else coming to make offerings, serve, or pay homage to them, he feels joy. He is endowed with right view and possesses a non-perverted perspective.

He held this view: that there is giving, merit, and recipients; that there are wholesome and unwholesome deeds; that there are this world and the next world; that there is father and mother; and that in the world there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life, as well as arhats who quickly realize and attain supernormal powers in this world and the next, and find delight therein.
Having achieved such excellent vision, at the time of death he will be reborn in the heavens.

It is as if a person were to go from one lecture hall to another, from one pavilion to another, or travel from one palace to another; for this reason, I say that such a person is excellent first and excellent later.
"In this way, that person is excellent at first and excellent later. Thus, Great King,
there are four types of persons who appear in the world."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Great King, when a person is poor and lowly, If they attain faith and delight in giving alms,
Upon seeing śramaṇas, brahmins, And all who come to beg for sustenance,”
Serving, honoring, and revering others, practicing all manner of wholesome deeds with equanimity,
always rejoicing at the sight of giving, and bestowing gifts even upon beggars—
this is the subtle and wondrous karma of generosity, which shall never again be stained by defilement.
Thus it is, O King, that when such a person approaches the end of life, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; first ugly, but later beautiful.
Great King, there are people who possess wealth, yet lack faith and harbor jealousy.
Constantly desiring to engage in improper conduct, Holding wrong views and having no teacher,
Upon seeing śramaṇas, brahmins, And various mendicants,
they slander and revile them constantly; Greedy and stingy as if they possessed no wealth, they remain so.
Seeing a gift being given, he obstructs it; when a beggar comes, he does not bestow charity.
His life is not a sublime action, and that person reaps defilement.
Thus, O King, when such a person is on the verge of death, his life ends in misery.
One will certainly be born and enter hell, having been exquisite at first and later becoming ugly.
O Great King, such a person is poor and lowly; lacking faith, with a stingy and greedy mind, they constantly desire to practice what is improper, holding wrong views and having no teacher.
Seeing śramaṇas and brahmins, as well as various beggars, they constantly revile and abuse them;
being stingy and greedy, they say they have no wealth, and when seeing an act of giving, they obstruct it; they do not bestow gifts upon those who beg.
His life was not of noble deeds; that person reaps defilement.
Thus, O King, when such a person is about to die, they will surely be reborn in hell—ugly at first and ugly thereafter.
Great King, you possess abundant wealth; being fond of faith, you constantly practice giving.
Upon seeing śramaṇas, brahmins, and all who come to beg, you serve, honor, and respect them, equally cultivating all manner of wholesome deeds.
Seeing a gift, one always rejoices; likewise, one bestows gifts upon those who beg.
This is a subtle and wondrous deed in this world, by which one no longer receives defilement.
Thus it is, O King, that when such a person is about to reach the end of life,
"Born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, one is sublime at first and sublime thereafter.
Therefore, Great King, you should train yourself in this way."
Thus it is, Great King!
You should train yourself in this way: to be excellent at first and excellent later; do not train yourself to be ugly at first and ugly later.
Thus it is, Great King!
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Sūtra on the Appearance of the Four Persons in the World*, as Spoken by the Buddha.
